name: Burlap-Ridge
geological_features: Rough-textured ridgelines covering most of the surface
Debris aprons from ancient ridge collapses
specific_features: Coarse, burlap-textured rock from unique weathering processes
Ridge system that forms a near-complete great circle around the equator
description: Burlap-Ridge is a small rocky world defined by a single massive ridge system that encircles the planet along the equator like a belt cinched around a stone waist. The ridge rises up to eight kilometers above the surrounding terrain, its flanks rough and textured with a coarse, fibrous appearance caused by differential weathering of layered basalt and sedimentary rock. The texture is strikingly similar to burlap fabric, with visible warp and weft patterns created by intersecting sets of rock strata exposed at the surface.

The ridge is the surface expression of an ancient tectonic compression event, likely caused by a change in the planet's rotation rate that concentrated stress along the equator. The thin atmosphere provides minimal erosion, preserving the ridge in something close to its original form, though micrometeorite bombardment has softened the highest points over billions of years. The terrain on either side of the ridge is relatively flat and featureless, impact-fractured bedrock covered in regolith, making the ridge itself the overwhelmingly dominant topographic feature.

The ridge creates interesting environmental gradients. Its altitude takes it above most of the thin atmosphere, creating even more extreme vacuum conditions at the summit than on the surrounding plains. The ridge flanks experience different solar heating depending on their orientation, creating temperature differentials that drive weak but persistent gas flows along the ridge—a threadbare substitute for wind in a world that can barely hold an atmosphere. These gas flows have, over billions of years, sculpted the burlap texture into patterns that follow prevailing flow directions, geological wind-vanes recording atmospheric currents too faint to detect directly.

Burlap-Ridge has modest economic value as a source of construction stone, with the layered basalt of the ridge providing structurally sound building material that can be quarried in the low gravity with minimal energy expenditure. The ridge also serves as a convenient navigation landmark for vessels transiting the local system. A small automated quarry operates on the ridge's northern face, cutting stone for use in habitat construction elsewhere in the system. The work is slow and methodical, shaving thin slices from a ridge that took billions of years to build, each block carrying the woven texture of deep time.
